facts.claim: At a Polterabend guests bring porcelain or stoneware (preferably) and smash it in front of the parental home of one partner or the couple's shared home, following the folk saying 'Scherben bringen Glück' (shards bring luck). Mirror shards, by contrast, are said to bring seven years of bad luck.
The engaged couple sweep up the broken shards together and throw them away.

The noise of the Polterabend is meant to drive away evil spirits and bring luck; in potters' usage 'Scherbe' originally meant any fired clay vessel, so the saying originally referred to full clay storage vessels (plentiful supplies) rather than broken pieces.

Historically the Polterabend was held the day before the church wedding; as the parties grew larger (from the 1950s, with 80 to 150 guests in the 1980s and 1990s) it moved to at least a week before the wedding and became a celebration in its own right. Invitations are traditionally not sent: word of mouth, and whoever comes is welcome.

The Polterabend is not celebrated everywhere: not every region has the tradition and not every couple holds one. 'Poltern' is imitative of a loud crashing noise (the same root as Poltergeist). Brauchwiki says other European countries such as Austria, Italy and Spain do not hold a separate Polterabend as Germany does.
facts.conflicts: No source found for the old page's 'pre-Christian' origin claim; label 'often told' or drop. A Saxony wedding portal snippet (search summary only) says the custom goes back to the 16th century: unverified.

facts.claim: The Hochzeitslader (also called Prograder, Progoder, Schmuser, Ehrvater or Hochzeitsbitter in different areas) historically went from guest to guest with a decorated rosewood staff to invite them, in the days before postal services.

The Hochzeitslader's staff is decorated with silk or paper ribbons; Brauchwiki gives red = love, blue = fidelity, green = hope, white = virginity. He recites a rhymed invitation at each house and could spend several weeks inviting everyone because each household offered him a drink and a snack.
facts.conflicts: BR gives white = innocence and adds yellow = jealousy, pink and light blue = children. Minor variation; writer can say colours carry wishes for the marriage.

facts.claim: Today door-to-door inviting by the Hochzeitslader is rarely practised (invitations are cards); the role is mostly on the day: forming the wedding procession, hosting, Gstanzl (humorous rhymed songs) about guests, games and organising.

Bavarian public broadcaster BR: in the Rupertiwinkel and Chiemgau, cattle dealers once matched couples and carried the invitations, hence the name Hochzeitslader (also Schmuser, Progoder). The custom is still widespread across south-east Bavaria; couples now book him for the day and he usually helps with preparations; he no longer matchmakes. BR says the first are said to date from the early 17th century.

Brauchwiki describes guests forming a Spalier (guard of honour) outside the church after the ceremony, meaning the couple must overcome the first 'obstacles' of marriage, and the bride being 'kidnapped' (Brautverziehen) during the Bavarian celebration, with the groom completing a task to get her back.

Brauchwiki is run by the Bayerischer Landesverein fuer Heimatpflege e.V. (Bavarian heritage association), founded in 2007 with the University of Augsburg's chair of European Ethnology/Folklore, under the patronage of the Bavarian State Ministry of Finance and Heritage, with an academic advisory board of folklore professors; user-submitted entries are checked by an editorial team. Basis for treating it as a regional heritage source.

The Junggesellenabschied is a celebration that sends the groom-to-be off from bachelor life (literally 'farewell to bachelorhood'); bachelorette versions (Junggesellinnenabschied) for brides are now also common.

Typical Junggesellenabschied: the group wears matching printed T-shirts, visits several pubs, and the groom must sell assorted small items to passers-by over the evening; weekend trips to a city or holiday region are increasingly popular.

Brauchwiki's Junggesellenabschied page adds that glass must never be smashed at a Polterabend because it is a symbol of bad luck, and repeats that the couple sweep the shards together. The same page calls the Polterabend 'probably' pre-Christian (vermutlich vorchristlich), without citing evidence.

The bride paying for her wedding shoes with saved pennies (Pfennige) dates from when women ran the household budget: girls saved from school age for their trousseau, and paying in saved coins showed a thrifty, steady wife. Brauchwiki says few girls save cents for this today; those who were girls in the 1970s and 1980s often still kept a jar of coins for it.

Brautschuh auction: sometimes a bride's shoe is secretly taken during the reception and auctioned among guests by a guest acting as auctioneer; the money is put in the shoe as it is passed round, and the bride gets the shoe and money back for the household budget.

'Something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue' is widespread in Germany but came from the English-speaking world (Victorian era); the German version usually drops the coin in the shoe ('silver sixpence'), so it is called the '4 Dinge der Braut'.

The long white wedding dress only became generally accepted in Germany in the 1930s (spreading from the cities); in rural areas a black festive dress with a white veil was worn for church weddings into the early 20th century.

insider_details.detail: A Polterabend is now usually held a week or more before the wedding rather than the night before, so for a destination wedding in Germany it can work as a separate welcome party for local friends, with a plan for noise and clean-up at the venue.
Bring guests porcelain or stoneware to smash, never glass or mirrors, and allow time for the couple to sweep up together, since that is part of the custom.

In south-east Bavaria (Chiemgau, Rupertiwinkel) couples still book a Hochzeitslader, who runs the procession, the timing and the humour on the day, much like an MC; an Australian couple marrying there can ask the venue whether one is used locally.
The shoe-coin custom is about thrift, not luck: it showed a bride could manage the household money, so it suits a story told in a speech rather than a ritual on the day.
Not every German region or couple holds a Polterabend, and many 'German' customs vary by area, so treat them as a menu rather than a checklist.
